subtopics.title: Centroid, centre of gravity and standard shapes
subtopics.theory_md:
**Centre of gravity (CG)** is the point through which the weight of a body acts; for a uniform plane lamina it coincides with the **centroid** of the area. A wire has its CG at the centroid of its **length**, not of the enclosed area.

Methods: (1) symmetry, (2) moments of simple parts, (3) integration, (4) graphical (force and funicular polygon), (5) experimental (suspend from two points, plumb line).

From the base: rectangle $d/2$, triangle $h/3$. Semicircle $\dfrac{4R}{3\pi}=0.424R$ from the diameter. Quadrant $\dfrac{4R}{3\pi}$ from each straight edge.
subtopics.basics_md: The centroid is the balance point of a flat plate. If the plate has a mirror line, it must balance on that line.
key_points: CG: point where the resultant weight acts; centroid for a plane area
Five methods: symmetry, moments, integration, graphical, experimental
Triangle h/3 from base; semicircle and quadrant 4R/3π
Wire (line) CG uses lengths; lamina uses areas

questions.q: The centroid of a triangle of height $h$ lies at what distance from its base?
questions.why: The medians meet at one third of the height from the base.

questions.q: The centroid of a semicircle of radius $R$ is at what distance from its diameter?
questions.why: $4R/3\pi=0.424R$; $2R/\pi$ is the value for a semicircular arc (wire), a common mix-up.

questions.q: Distinguish between centre of gravity and centroid.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Centre of gravity** is the point through which the resultant weight of a body acts in every orientation.

**Centroid** is the geometric centre of a line, area or volume.

For a homogeneous body of uniform thickness the two coincide; for a body of varying density the CG shifts towards the denser part while the centroid does not.
points: CG is the point of action of the weight
Centroid is a purely geometric centre
They coincide for a homogeneous body of uniform thickness

questions.q: Find the distance of the centroid of a quadrant of a circle of radius $R=100$ mm from each straight edge.
questions.model_answer_md: $\bar x=\bar y=\dfrac{4R}{3\pi}=\dfrac{4\times100}{3\pi}=42.44$ mm from each straight edge.

points: CG is the point of action of the resultant weight; centroid for a plane area
Moments of composite parts with formulas, holes negative
Graphical (force and funicular polygon) and experimental (suspension, plumb line) methods
Area centroid at h/3 from the base
Wire CG: BC (2l) at 0, AB and AC (L each) at h/2

subtopics.title: Composite lamina by the method of moments
subtopics.theory_md:
Split the lamina into rectangles, triangles, semicircles and so on. Take axes at a corner (or the base and a symmetry line). For each part write area $a$ and its centroid $(x,y)$. A **hole or cut-out is a negative area**.
$$\bar x=\frac{\sum a x}{\sum a},\qquad \bar y=\frac{\sum a y}{\sum a}$$
Set out a table: part, $a$, $x$, $y$, $ax$, $ay$. If an axis of symmetry exists, the centroid lies on it, so one coordinate is free.
subtopics.basics_md: Every part pulls the balance point towards itself, in proportion to its area. A hole pulls with negative strength, so the balance point moves away from it.
key_points: Split into standard shapes with known areas and centroids
Hole or cut-out entered as negative area
Table of a, x, y, ax, ay and the two divisions
Use a symmetry axis to save one coordinate
State the answer with the reference origin and units

subtopics.title: Centroid by integration
subtopics.theory_md:
Take an elemental strip $dA$ and the coordinates of **its own centroid** $(x_c,y_c)$:
$$\bar x=\frac{\int x_c\,dA}{\int dA},\quad \bar y=\frac{\int y_c\,dA}{\int dA}$$
Vertical strip of height $y$ and width $dx$: $dA=y\,dx$, $x_c=x$, $y_c=y/2$. Horizontal strip: $dA=x\,dy$, $x_c=x/2$, $y_c=y$. Between two curves use $y_1-y_2$ and the mean height $(y_1+y_2)/2$.
For $y=kx^n$ under the curve up to $(a,b)$: $\bar x=\dfrac{n+1}{n+2}a$, $\bar y=\dfrac{n+1}{4n+2}b$.
subtopics.basics_md: Chop the area into thin strips, find each strip's tiny moment, add them up (integrate) and divide by the total area.
key_points: Choose strip, write dA and strip's own centroid
Integrate A, ∫x dA and ∫y dA between the limits
Divide to get x-bar and y-bar
Between two curves: height y1 - y2, mean height (y1+y2)/2
Check with a known case (n = 1 triangle gives 2a/3, b/3)

questions.q: Find the centroid of the area under the parabola $y=x^2$ from $x=0$ to $x=3$ and the x-axis.
questions.model_answer_md:
Vertical strip: $dA=y\,dx=x^2dx$, centroid $(x,\ x^2/2)$.

$A=\int_0^3x^2dx=9$

$\int x\,dA=\int_0^3x^3dx=\dfrac{81}{4}$, so $\bar x=\dfrac{81/4}{9}=2.25$

$\int \dfrac y2\,dA=\int_0^3\dfrac{x^4}{2}dx=\dfrac{243}{10}$, so $\bar y=\dfrac{24.3}{9}=2.7$

Centroid $(2.25,\ 2.7)$. Check with $n=2$, $a=3$, $b=9$: $\tfrac34a=2.25$, $\tfrac3{10}b=2.7$.
points: Vertical strip dA = x² dx, centroid (x, x²/2)
k = b/a^n from the point (a, b)
k = a/b³; horizontal strip of length (a - ky³)
Intersection of y = 3x/2 and y = x²/4 at x = 0 and x = 6
Divide into elements; sum of moments equals moment of total weight
x-bar = ∫x dW/∫dW, same for y and z; lamina uses dA
Steps: axes, element and its centroid, integrate, divide
Example: rectangle b/2 or triangle h/3
Half-width at height y is y/√3, dA = 2y dy/√3

subtopics.title: Moment of inertia, polar moment and radius of gyration
subtopics.theory_md:
**Moment of inertia (second moment) of an area** about an axis in its plane: $I_{xx}=\int y^2\,dA$, $I_{yy}=\int x^2\,dA$. Unit $\mathrm{mm^4}$, always positive; it measures resistance to bending ($M/I=\sigma/y$).

**Polar moment** about an axis perpendicular to the plane through O: $I_P=J=\int r^2dA=I_{xx}+I_{yy}$; it measures resistance to twisting ($T/J=\tau/r$).

**Radius of gyration** $k=\sqrt{I/A}$, so $I=Ak^2$.
subtopics.basics_md: Area far from an axis counts for much more than area near it, because the distance is squared.
key_points: I = ∫y² dA, unit length⁴, always positive
Polar J = ∫r² dA = Ixx + Iyy, axis perpendicular to plane
Ixx relates to bending, J to torsion
Radius of gyration k = √(I/A)

questions.q: The SI unit of moment of inertia of an area is
questions.why: Area times length squared gives length to the fourth. $\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ is the mass moment of inertia.

points: I = ∫y² dA, ∫x² dA; unit mm⁴; always positive; k = √(I/A)
Polar I = ∫r² dA about axis perpendicular to plane, equals Ixx + Iyy
Relates to torsion; circle J = πd⁴/32

subtopics.title: Derivations of standard sections
subtopics.theory_md:
Strip method: $I_{xx}=\int y^2\,dA$ with $dA$ = width x $dy$.
- Rectangle: $\dfrac{bd^3}{12}$ centroidal, $\dfrac{bd^3}{3}$ about the base.
- Triangle: $\dfrac{bh^3}{12}$ about base, $\dfrac{bh^3}{36}$ centroidal (shift by $h/3$).
- Circle: ring $dA=2\pi r\,dr$, $J=\dfrac{\pi R^4}{2}$, so $I_{diameter}=\dfrac{\pi R^4}{4}=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{64}$.
- Semicircle: $\dfrac{\pi R^4}{8}$ about the diameter, $0.1098R^4$ centroidal.
- Trapezium (parallel sides $a$ base, $b$ top): $I_{base}=\dfrac{h^3(a+3b)}{12}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Slice the shape into thin strips parallel to the axis; each strip has area (width x thickness) and distance y. Add y² dA.
key_points: Strip parallel to the axis, dA = width x dy
Rectangle bd³/12 and bd³/3; triangle bh³/12 base and bh³/36 centroidal
Circle πd⁴/64 via ring J = πR⁴/2 and symmetry
Semicircle πR⁴/8 about diameter
Trapezium h³(a+3b)/12 about its base

questions.q: A triangle has base 120 mm and height 90 mm. Find $I$ about its base and about the centroidal axis parallel to the base.

$A=\dfrac{\pi(40)^2}{2}=2513.3\ \mathrm{mm^2}$, centroid $\dfrac{4R}{3\pi}=16.98$ mm from the diameter.

$I_G=1.005\times10^6-2513.3\times16.98^2=0.281\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$ (that is $0.1098R^4$).

I_G = I - A y² = 0.281 x 10⁶ mm⁴
Perpendicular axis: J = 2 Ixx, so Ixx = πR⁴/4 = πd⁴/64
Substitute y = R sin θ to get πR⁴/4
Or: ring J = πR⁴/2 halved by symmetry

subtopics.title: Moment of inertia about a diagonal
subtopics.theory_md:
An axis along a diagonal splits a rectangle into **two equal triangles, each with the diagonal as base**. So
$$I_{diag}=2\times\frac{(\text{base})\,h^3}{12}$$
where base $=\sqrt{b^2+d^2}$ and the height of each triangle (perpendicular from the corner to the diagonal) $=\dfrac{bd}{\sqrt{b^2+d^2}}$. This gives
$$I_{diag}=\frac{b^3d^3}{6(b^2+d^2)}$$
For a square of side $a$: $a^4/12$, the same as any centroidal axis.
subtopics.basics_md: Cut along the diagonal: each half is a triangle sitting on the diagonal. A triangle about its own base is bh³/12.
key_points: Diagonal divides rectangle into two triangles on that base
Base = √(b²+d²), height = bd/√(b²+d²)
I = b³d³/(6(b²+d²)); square gives a⁴/12

questions.why: Equal to the value about a centroidal axis parallel to a side, since all centroidal axes of a square are equivalent.

questions.q: Find the moment of inertia of a rectangle 4 cm by 3 cm about its diagonal.
questions.model_answer_md:

$I=2\times\dfrac{5\times2.4^3}{12}=11.52\ \mathrm{cm^4}$

Check: $\dfrac{b^3d^3}{6(b^2+d^2)}=\dfrac{64\times27}{6\times25}=11.52$.
points: Two triangles on the diagonal as base
Diagonal splits rectangle into two equal triangles
I = 2 x AC h³/12 = b³d³/(6(b² + d²))
Diagonal a√2 splits the square into two triangles of height a/√2

subtopics.title: Product of inertia
subtopics.theory_md:
**Product of inertia** $I_{xy}=\int xy\,dA$. Unlike $I_{xx}$ it can be **positive, negative or zero**; unit $\mathrm{mm^4}$.
- If either axis is an **axis of symmetry**, $I_{xy}=0$.
- Parallel axis: $I_{xy}=I_{x'y'}+A\bar x\bar y$, with $\bar x,\bar y$ the centroid coordinates (with sign) in the new axes.
- Rectangle $b\times d$ about two edges at a corner: $\dfrac{b^2d^2}{4}$.
Sign: positive if the area lies mostly in quadrants 1 and 3, negative if in 2 and 4.
subtopics.basics_md: Each bit of area contributes x times y. Area in the upper-right or lower-left adds; area in the other two quadrants subtracts.
key_points: Ixy = ∫xy dA, may be + , - or 0
Zero if either axis is a symmetry axis
Transfer: Ixy = Ix'y' + A x-bar y-bar (signed)
Rectangle at corner: b²d²/4

questions.why: Contributions of the two mirror halves cancel.

questions.q: A lamina lies entirely in the second quadrant of the axes. Its $I_{xy}$ is
questions.why: There $x<0$ and $y>0$, so every $xy$ is negative.

questions.q: A rectangle 60 mm by 40 mm has its 60 mm side along the x-axis and its 40 mm side along the y-axis, with one corner at the origin. Find $I_{xy}$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Centroidal $I_{x'y'}=0$ (symmetry). Centroid $(30,\ 20)$ mm, $A=2400\ \mathrm{mm^2}$.

$I_{xy}=0+A\bar x\bar y=2400\times30\times20=1.44\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$

Check: $b^2d^2/4=3600\times1600/4=1.44\times10^6$.
points: Use A x-bar y-bar with centroid (30, 20)

subtopics.title: Principal axes and principal moments
subtopics.theory_md:
**Principal axes** are the pair of perpendicular axes about which $I_{xy}=0$ and $I$ is maximum on one and minimum on the other. For an area with an axis of symmetry, that axis and its perpendicular are principal.
$$\tan2\theta_p=\frac{-2I_{xy}}{I_{xx}-I_{yy}}$$
$$I_{max,min}=\frac{I_{xx}+I_{yy}}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{I_{xx}-I_{yy}}{2}\right)^2+I_{xy}^2}$$
$I_{max}+I_{min}=I_{xx}+I_{yy}$ always. Mohr's circle: centre at $(I_{xx}+I_{yy})/2$, radius the root above.
subtopics.basics_md: Rotate the axes and I changes. There is one direction where it is largest and the perpendicular direction where it is smallest; there, Ixy vanishes.
key_points: Principal axes: Ixy = 0, I is max and min
tan 2θ = -2Ixy/(Ixx - Iyy), two roots 90 degrees apart
Imax,min = average ± √(((Ixx - Iyy)/2)² + Ixy²)
Imax + Imin = Ixx + Iyy
Symmetry axes are principal axes

questions.why: Principal axes are defined by $I_{xy}=0$.

questions.q: For any pair of perpendicular axes through the same point, $I_{xx}+I_{yy}$ is
questions.why: The sum is the polar moment about the point and does not depend on rotation.

questions.q: For a section, $I_{xx}=8000\ \mathrm{cm^4}$, $I_{yy}=2000\ \mathrm{cm^4}$ and $I_{xy}=-2000\ \mathrm{cm^4}$ about its centroid. Find the principal moments and the inclination of the principal axis of $I_{max}$ to the x-axis.

subtopics.title: Statement and proof
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** the moment of inertia of an area about any axis in its plane equals the moment of inertia about a **parallel centroidal axis** plus the **area times the square of the distance** between the axes: $I_{AB}=I_G+Ah^2$.

**Proof:** an element $dA$ is at $y$ from the centroidal axis G-G, so at $(h+y)$ from AB.
$$I_{AB}=\int(h+y)^2dA=h^2\!\int dA+2h\!\int y\,dA+\int y^2dA=Ah^2+0+I_G$$
$\int y\,dA=0$ because it is the first moment about the centroidal axis. Draw the sketch: area with centroid G, axes GG and AB, element at $y$.
subtopics.basics_md: Moving the axis away from the centroid always increases I by A times distance squared; the centroidal value is the smallest of all parallel axes.
key_points: Statement: I_AB = I_G + A h²
Sketch with G-G, AB, h, element dA at y
Expand (h + y)²
∫y dA = 0 about a centroidal axis
Result I_AB = I_G + A h²

questions.q: In $I_{AB}=I_G+Ah^2$, the axis G-G must
options: be the neutral axis of the beam
questions.why: The cross term vanishes only because the first moment about G-G is zero.

questions.q: Among all parallel axes, the moment of inertia is least about
options: any axis through the middle of a side
questions.why: Every other axis adds $Ah^2\ge0$.

questions.q: Why does the cross term $2h\int y\,dA$ vanish in the proof of the parallel axis theorem?
questions.model_answer_md: $\int y\,dA=A\bar y$ is the first moment of the area about the axis G-G. G-G passes through the centroid, so $\bar y=0$ and the term is zero. This is why one of the two axes must be centroidal.
points: ∫y dA is the first moment about G-G
Centroid lies on G-G, so it is zero
Hence one axis must be centroidal
Sketch: area, centroid G, axes GG and AB, element at y
Statement with centroidal axis, A and h
Proof by expansion of ∫(h + y)² dA
I_AB = I_G + A h²; example rectangle bd³/3

subtopics.title: Using the theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
Use it to move an axis **from or to the centroid**, never directly between two non-centroidal axes without passing through G.

Two non-centroidal axes: $I_2=I_1-Ah_1^2+Ah_2^2$ (first go down to $I_G$, then up).

Examples: rectangle about base $\dfrac{bd^3}{3}$; circle of diameter $d$ about a tangent $\dfrac{5\pi d^4}{64}$; triangle about base $\dfrac{bh^3}{12}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Always route through the centroid: down to I_G, then up to the new axis. The area in the formula is the whole area.
key_points: Only one of the two axes can be non-centroidal in one step
Two off-centroid axes: subtract A h1², add A h2²
Circle about tangent 5πd⁴/64
h is the perpendicular distance between the parallel axes

A section of area $2000\ \mathrm{mm^2}$ has $I=4.2\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$ about an axis 30 mm from its centroid. Find $I$ about a parallel axis 50 mm from the centroid on the opposite side.

Then out: $I=2.4\times10^6+2000\times50^2=7.4\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$.

The side does not matter: only the square of the distance.
points: Go down to the centroid first: I_G = 2.4 x 10⁶ mm⁴
Then add A h² with h = 50 mm

subtopics.title: Statement and proof
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** for a plane area, the moment of inertia about an axis **perpendicular to the plane** through O equals the sum of the moments of inertia about **two perpendicular axes in the plane meeting at O**: $I_{ZZ}=I_{XX}+I_{YY}$.

**Proof:** sketch the lamina in the x-y plane, OZ perpendicular at O, element $dA$ at $(x,y)$ and distance $r$ from O, $r^2=x^2+y^2$.
$$I_{ZZ}=\int r^2dA=\int(x^2+y^2)dA=\int x^2dA+\int y^2dA=I_{YY}+I_{XX}$$
Applies to plane areas (laminae) only.
subtopics.basics_md: Distance from O is the hypotenuse of x and y, and squares add like Pythagoras.
key_points: Statement: Izz = Ixx + Iyy
Sketch with OX, OY in the plane, OZ perpendicular, element at (x, y), r
r² = x² + y²
Result by splitting the integral
Valid for plane laminae only

questions.why: It relies on $r^2=x^2+y^2$ for an element lying in a plane.

questions.q: In $I_{ZZ}=I_{XX}+I_{YY}$, the axes X and Y

questions.q: State the perpendicular axis theorem. Why does it not apply to a three-dimensional body?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Statement:** for a plane area, $I_{ZZ}=I_{XX}+I_{YY}$ with X and Y perpendicular in the plane and Z perpendicular to it, all through O.

It rests on $r^2=x^2+y^2$ for an element lying in the plane (all of its $z$ is zero). For a solid, elements lie at different $z$, so $r^2$ about Z is not $x^2+y^2$ alone for the other axes.
points: Uses r² = x² + y² for an element in the plane
Neat sketch: lamina, axes X, Y in the plane, Z perpendicular, element dA at (x, y), r
Result; example circle πd⁴/32 = 2 x πd⁴/64

subtopics.title: Using the theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
Gives the **polar moment** from two in-plane values, or one in-plane value from the polar value when symmetry makes $I_{XX}=I_{YY}$.
- Circle: $J=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{32}$, so $I_{XX}=I_{YY}=\dfrac{\pi d^4}{64}$.
- Hollow circle: $J=\dfrac{\pi(D^4-d^4)}{32}$.
- Rectangle: $J=\dfrac{bd(b^2+d^2)}{12}$.
A rectangle has $I_{XX}\ne I_{YY}$, so $J$ alone cannot give either.
subtopics.basics_md: Only symmetry lets you halve J: for a circle, every diameter is the same.
key_points: J = Ixx + Iyy
Circle: Ixx = J/2 by symmetry
Rectangle: J = bd(b² + d²)/12
Cannot halve J when Ixx ≠ Iyy

topics.topic: Moment of inertia of composite areas

subtopics.title: Cut-out sections about the centroidal axis
subtopics.theory_md:
For a shape with semicircle, triangle or rectangle added or cut:
1. **Centroid** $\bar y$ from the base by the table (cut-outs negative).
2. **I about the base** (or any convenient axis): standard formulas, cut-outs subtracted. Semicircle about its diameter $\dfrac{\pi R^4}{8}$; triangle about base $\dfrac{bh^3}{12}$; rectangle on base $\dfrac{bd^3}{3}$.
3. **Shift:** $I_{XX}=I_{base}-A\bar y^2$, with $A$ the net area.
For a semicircle or triangle not on the axis, use $I=I_G+ah^2$ with $I_G=0.1098R^4$ or $bh^3/36$.
subtopics.basics_md: Find the balance point, take I about an easy line (the base), then come back to the balance point with the parallel axis theorem.
key_points: Step 1: centroid by table, cut-outs negative
Step 2: I about the base, cut-outs subtracted
Step 3: I_XX = I_base - A ybar² with net A
Part not on the axis: I_G + a h²
Final answer in mm⁴ with units

questions.q: A rectangle 100 mm wide and 60 mm deep has a circular hole of diameter 40 mm at its centre. Find $I_{xx}$ about the horizontal centroidal axis.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both are centred, so the centroid is unchanged at the rectangle centre.

$I_{rect}=\dfrac{100\times60^3}{12}=1.8\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$

$I_{hole}=\dfrac{\pi(40)^4}{64}=0.1257\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$

$I_{xx}=1.8\times10^6-0.1257\times10^6=1.674\times10^6\ \mathrm{mm^4}$

subtopics.title: Moment of inertia about a given axis
subtopics.theory_md:
When the question names the axis (AB, LM, an edge), **no centroid is needed**. Take each part's I about **that** axis: $I=I_G+ah^2$ with $h$ the distance from the part's centroid to AB. Add the solid parts, **subtract** the holes and cut-outs.

Radius of gyration about that axis: $k=\sqrt{I_{AB}/A}$ with $A$ the net area.
Standard: triangle on AB $\dfrac{bh^3}{12}$, rectangle on AB $\dfrac{bd^3}{3}$, semicircle on its diameter $\dfrac{\pi R^4}{8}$, circle centred on AB $\dfrac{\pi d^4}{64}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Do not look for the centroid unless asked. Measure every distance from the given axis and use the parallel axis theorem part by part.
key_points: Use the axis given, no composite centroid
I of each part = I_G + a h² about that axis
Subtract holes and cut-outs
k = √(I/A) with net area
Check that a hole lies inside the lamina

subtopics.title: Built-up and hollow sections (T, I, Z, channel, box)
subtopics.theory_md:
Split into rectangles. **Symmetric about X-X:** centroid at mid-depth. **Z-section:** two equal flanges give the centroid at the centre of the web. Otherwise find $\bar y$ by the table.
$$I_{XX}=\sum\left(\frac{bd^3}{12}+ah^2\right)$$
with $h$ = distance of each part's centroid from X-X. A hollow rectangle: $\dfrac{BD^3-bd^3}{12}$. Tapered flange: rectangle plus triangle ($bh^3/36+ah^2$). Cut-outs on a side: semicircle about its own centroid, then transfer.
subtopics.basics_md: Each rectangle contributes its own bd³/12 plus a h² for how far it sits from the axis. Wide flanges far from the axis give most of the I.
key_points: Divide into rectangles, state b, d and a
Centroid by table (mid-depth if symmetric, centre of web for Z)
Ixx = Σ(bd³/12 + a h²)
Hollow section: outer minus inner
Tapered flange: rectangle plus triangle
Units and final value
